page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 2 marks

steps.label: The two definitions
lines: Arrhenius acid: a substance that gives H⁺
Arrhenius base: a substance that gives OH⁻
steps.why: The Arrhenius theory defines acid and base by the ion each releases IN WATER — H⁺ for acids, OH⁻ for bases. The phrase 'in aqueous solution' is part of both definitions.
common_mistakes: Leaving out 'in aqueous solution'. The theory is defined for water only.
Writing proton acceptor for the base. The Arrhenius base gives OH⁻; proton acceptor is Brønsted-Lowry.
steps.memory_tip: The Arrhenius definitions hold in water only: acid gives H⁺, base gives OH⁻, both in aqueous solution.
steps.margin_note: Both definitions end with the same three words: in aqueous solution.

steps.label: Examples and limitation
lines: Limitation: the theory applies only to
aqueous solutions, and it cannot explain
the basic nature of substances without
steps.why: HCl and NaOH are the clearest examples — full ionisation in water into H⁺ and OH⁻. The NH₃ limitation is why the later theories were needed. This single mark covers the two examples AND the limitation together, so write both parts.
common_mistakes: Giving NH₃ as an Arrhenius base. NH₃ has no OH⁻ — it is the standard counter-example.
Writing an example without naming which theory member it is.
steps.memory_tip: HCl and NaOH are the standard pair. NH₃ is the counter-example the Arrhenius theory cannot explain.
steps.margin_note: One example each, then the limitation line. Both parts sit inside this one mark.

insider_note: The second mark is one row holding the examples and the limitation together, so both have to be written. NH₃ is the limitation that row is looking for, and it is also the wrong answer if it is given as a base.
